title: ‘Show How 3M Is 0% at Fault:’ Expert Witness Used ChatGPT to Write Report Defending Company in Deadly Explosion Lawsuit

reading.body:
The failure here is an expert witness using a general-purpose language model to produce a forensic report in adversarial litigation, with the model directed by a prompt that stated a conclusion before any analysis occurred. Asking a chatbot to "show how" a party is zero percent at fault is not analysis, it is confabulation working backward from a desired outcome. The deployment happened at the point of report authorship, before the document entered the court record, meaning no independent technical review caught that the reasoning was constructed to fit a predetermined result rather than derived from evidence.

The failure mode is a model asserting conclusions as expert findings when the input prompt foreclosed any other answer. A genuine expert analysis would begin from evidence and reach a conclusion, but here the conclusion was embedded in the instruction. That inversion is not detectable from the finished report alone, which is why the prompts themselves had to surface through discovery before the problem became visible.

What is not established is whether the report's specific technical conclusions are wrong on the merits, whether any court has ruled the report inadmissible, and whether 3M knew or directed how the report was produced.

reports.title: ‘Show How 3M Is 0% at Fault:’ Expert Witness Used ChatGPT to Write Report Defending Company in Deadly Explosion Lawsuit

summary:
An expert witness hired by 3M to defend the company in a lawsuit over a deadly 2020 Houston explosion used ChatGPT to write major portions of his expert report. The witness's AI prompts, which became publicly available through court documents, revealed he asked the chatbot to create a report showing that 3M was zero percent at fault for the blast at Watson Grinding. The explosion killed three people and destroyed roughly 200 homes, spawning a 61 million dollar lawsuit.

The incident demonstrates how artificial intelligence has entered courtrooms beyond legal briefs and now includes expert witness testimony in high-stakes cases involving significant liability. The 2020 explosion was caused by a degraded rubber welding hose that leaked flammable gas. Plaintiffs allege that 3M failed to properly maintain the facility's gas detection system and made other errors contributing to the disaster. The case reveals that the specific prompts used to generate expert testimony can be discovered during litigation, potentially embarrassing those who created them.
